comments.body: I understand why this jury could not agree on a verdict too. As a Massachusetts resident with friends on both sides of the political divide, I can inform you many Massachusetts residents agree the DA never should have brought this as a first-degree murder case. He did this in a similar case before the same judge. The guilty verdict against that mother came after the judge ruled inadmissible evidence of the mother's medical records showing she too suffered from extreme mental illness. The state's high court recently ordered a new trial in that case. I am not a mother and have never experienced post-partum psychosis.  Regardless, I could never find beyond a reasonable doubt what was in this mother's mind. I have the greatest respect for this jury and thank God I wasn't on it.

comments.name: Suzanna
comments.body:
Mother's are so often maligned in the criminal justice system. Although vastly different, I am reminded of Lindy Chamberlain (of "a dingo ate my baby" fame), where her demeanor in court was used against her. How is a grieving mother supposed to act? If she wails and screams, it's histrionics and she's putting on a show. If she's quiet and subdued, she's distant and uncaring. If she smiles or laughs, even once, she's apparently glad that her children are dead.

I don't know what happened that fateful day, but I believe there was considerable reasonable doubt and acquittal was the only appropriate option. I hope she isn't retried. Even if she did kill her children (which I have doubts about), she did so under such great emotional distress that she will now spend the rest of her life paralyzed, likely in a forensic hospital, and with feelings of shame and loss she will never rid herself of.

It is so immensely sad that so many lives were lost and ruined, but I hope this case will at least open up the conversation on postpartum depression and psychosis. These are real disorders, and while PPP is rare, it affects 1000s of mothers, putting them, their children, and their families at risk. Better recognition of warning signs and better policies for intervention need to be established. Although I have doubts Lindsey killed her children, it is clear she was suffering and scared. I hope she finally gets the help she asked for so many times.

This article is irresponsibly phrased, peppered with words that overly personify an LLM (which is nothing more than a machine that is really good at predicting the next word, pixel, or line of code) with human characteristics. No machine “decided” to do anything. No machine “colluded”, “assumed leadership roles”, or any other complex human behavior. To label what the LLMs did in this way is to give too much power to their creators, OpenAI, and helps advance the “AI Doomers” narrative that AI is both inevitable and catastrophic. Both Emily Bender and Cory Doctorow, among others, have pointed out that the Doomer fantasy of rogue AI, fueled by humans strange fascination with the personifying machine characteristics, feeds in to the AI industry’s need to make LLMs SEEM hyper intelligent. It fuels the need for more and more capital to build ever more complex models. In fact foundation models are not at all hyper intelligent; rather they are amazing prediction machines that are being asked to solve cybersecurity problems and nothing more. These are absolutely NOT sentient machines. So let’s please stop using language imbuing them with sentient powers they don’t have. 

Let’s absolutely report what LLMs are doing, and hold the creators of them to account. But let’s also report and hold accountable using terms and framing that is accurate, not adding human-sounding characteristics to what is ultimately just a really good prediction machine.

Index to local wages. Set the floor at a percentage of each metro area's median wage rather than one statewide figure. At $16.90, the floor barely affects San Jose - but it bites hard in Bakersfield — same law, opposite effects, and the poorer region takes the loss.  Then put it on autopilot.

Evaluation written into the statute. Sunset clause, pre-registered analysis plan, mandatory microdata access for outside researchers, automatic review before renewal.

Adversarial collaboration. Fund economists with differing views to specify one analysis jointly, in advance, and publish whatever it yields.

A standing wage commission. Britain's Low Pay Commission — employers, unions, and academics, recommending a rate each year against an explicit mandate to avoid employment harm — has taken this question substantially out of British electoral politics for twenty-five years.

Separate the goal from the instrument. If the objective is income for low-wage households, the EITC (Earned Income Tax Credit) reaches it with less collateral damage and better targeting — a substantial share of minimum-wage earners are second earners in non-poor households, and the wage floor puts the entire cost on one narrow class of employers. There were black walnut, hawthorn, persimmon and cedar trees all around the place along with a small artesian spring fed pond.  The spring head was in a small coolaired recess that had hanging grape vines large enough to swing on and over the little creek.  Another seasonal pond always had sacs of tadpoles in the spring and huge bullfrogs later on, it froze over now and then usually into a rough rippled skating rink.  I did not know of Mr. Berry until later in my life and long after we moved from that beautiful area of Kentucky and, to which I returned once.  The trees were now cut, that wonderful spring with its crawdads hiding under glacial flat rocks that sometimes would revel what looked like embedded trilobite fossils - paved over, the bank barn demolished too.   But I deeply understand how he felt.

When I was young, you could take a 20 minute drive and see multiple farms with cows grazing in the fields.  Now, cows are a rare sight around here.  I get it, that milk is a subsidized commodity, and the price is pretty much what it was 50 years ago.  But property taxes, tractor prices, labor, fuel, building maintenance,  feed, seed, and everything else associated with farming has skyrocketed!  On top of it, dairy farming is a 24/7/365 proposition.  Nowadays, a farmer with 30-50 head of cattle simply cannot survive.  It is very sad.  Small scale farming has given way to agribusiness.  I applaud the Mareb's for doing what they do, and the commitment they made.  And anyone else who puts in the effort to run and maintain a farm, farm land, and anything else that goes along with the long hours associated with it.  It is not a job for the weary.  It is not something to dive into, unless you are in 100%.   Farms are the lifeblood for the world, and should be treated and respected as such.  We should all commit to keeping them going, and encourage those that want to see it happen!

comments.name: MG
comments.body: The whole point of the Mercator map is it solved an actual problem. Sailors used it to plot straight line courses across oceans without constantly adjusting their compass. People’s lives depended on it. That’s why it stuck around for 450 years, not because some cartographer in 1569 was trying to make Africa look small. Now we’ve got 164 countries at the UN voting to replace it with a map that solves what exactly? Google already ditched Mercator for a 3D globe on desktop back in 2018. The resolution literally uses phrases like “cognitive justice” and “memorial reparation” — that tells you everything about what this is actually about. It’s not about better maps. It’s about making a political statement dressed up as cartography.

comments.name: Flossymoo

Maps are invariably political objects, and you will never make anybody happy with just one. My vote is to have at least three that you use to educate, so that when you learn about the Earth, you learn about it through the many views you can have of it. Perhaps the answer here isn’t just about changing the map, it’s about educating alongside it as to what maps are, what they do, and what they can represent? For the record, as an Australian, I am pretty fed up with us always being on the far edge and distorted, and that’s if we are even included - the number of media representations in places like the US that completely forget about us existing at all is mind boggling.

Come to think of it, why would Americans bother about a world map anyway? Everyone across the world knows that, for Americans, there’s only one country, completely surrounded by water, because nowhere and nobody else on the planet is worth knowing about… unless you can bomb it, of course.

The overall theme was how blessed Africa was geographically. A continent that hardly suffers from the natural disasters that bedevils other continents. 
That song was a rejection of everything we've been made to believe about the continent of Africa including the falsehoods about the people, its history, its culture, natural resources and the righting of a cartographic error o 2026 - between late than never. And especially during a time when the books we all relied on kids back in those days were written by these Europeans - talk about a colonial brain wash.

Many clinical trials, taken in aggregate especially, have shown a direct correlation between LDL  ("bad" cholesterol) lowering and prevention of cardiovascular events, such that for every 39 point lowering of LDL, there will be a 22% reduction in events. So let's not confuse this extremely well-supported data with the new Novartis drug findings, which apply ONLY to Lp(a),  a special type of LDL-like molecule which is significantly elevated in about 20% of the population, and correlates (separately from LDL) with enhanced heart attack risk. Lowering Lp(a) specifically is not at all the same as lowering LDL. Lowering LDL saves lives. Lowering Lp(a) apparently does not, despite the correlation with bad outcomes at high Lp(a) levels. So statin drugs will lower LDL  and save lives, per well-established evidence. Non-statin LDL-lowering drugs also have some clinical trial evidence for better outcomes. The new drug that lowers Lp(a) successfully just produces  a lower Lp(a) number, not a longer life free of heart attack. Concentrating even harder on lowering LDL makes the most sense for those with high Lp(a), along with controlling other cardiovascular risk factors like tobacco use, high blood pressure and diabetes.

Niacin (raises HDL or "good cholesterol) and folic acid (lowers homocysteine levels) have similar track records to the Novartis drug--better numbers, no better outcomes

comments.body: I'm a racer, and also have worked as a racing instructor and a racing coach. As such, I try and help the average person understand the many factors leading to success. IAt first, I insist they drive a simple 'safe line" until they know the course, then they can blend more to the 'fast line" that is riskier and requires them to look "thru the corner". That's where the ability to see in 3D and anticipate via visual memory comes into play. Some just don't have it, others do. The SIM video with eye trace shows that, BUT, that's a luxury as a driver. In the real world, on track, we are far busier: We are looking at cars ahead..is that smoke coming from an engine letting go? Oil down? Or we are planning when and where we will catch that car, then looking behind us, how much gap do I have? Sometimes you want to ease your pace to catch the slower car at a location where you can get by quickly, instead of getting stuck with no momentum and having your competitor behind close the gap. That's racecraft. Also, often there are faster cars in different classes, so the mirrors must be checked constantly. Which means eyes not on the track ahead. The car  needs monitoring, as most don't have a team watching the cars data via telemetry, that's my job. Having to take avoiding action to not hit a spinning car might result in a trip across the grass. Smart drivers know grass clippings can clog the radiator, so extra vigilance is needed to watch oil and H2O temps. the brain is busy out there!

The author states that MAID allows physicians to “administer lethal medication to patients who have a terminal diagnosis ....” Physicians are PRESCRIBING the medication, not administering it. There’s a BIG difference. Nowhere in the US can a provider legally administer MAID medication. The patient MUST self-administer.

Later, he writes that physicians need drugs “to end the lives of their patients.”  Mr. Cohen, physicians are not the primary actors in this. Doctors are not ENDING their patients’ lives. After assessing eligibility, they are fulfilling an autonomous patient request.

Words matter. For people curious about MAID, this language misinforms and frightens. It also disserves those at Quiĕtus and others in NY who worked tirelessly to prepare for MAID implementation.

Even the quote—“you’re representing relief, but you’re also representing horror”—feels intentional. In my research with families whose loved ones used MAID, I have heard extraordinary gratitude for the medical providers who supported them.

Regarding Dr. Dugdale’s desire to help patients “flourish even as their bodies decay”: as a caregiver for 13 years, I know patients can only “flourish” so far. Unless we inhabit that patient’s body, we cannot determine what flourishing means for them.

This piece is skeptical of MAID. But skepticism is one thing; distorting facts is another. Exaggerating the physician’s role when reaching millions crosses from perspective into misinformation.

Do better, NYT.
